How do you build a company harness?
We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives:
It lives where people already work (for us that's Slack)
It knows who's asking and acts OBO that person for some services and with its own identity for others
It has memory, scoped globally and/or at the user level
Code runs in a sandbox and can make requests to services which require auth
Large % of its runs are scheduled rather than explicitly invoked by someone (ambient agents!!)
Thank you to @caspar_br for help on this blog
LangChain Internal Agents
To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain:
GTM Agent: a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions
OpenSWE: our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs
Content Studio: our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning
All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses.
Problem: User Experience
All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps, and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it.
One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel.
There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI.
Problem: Identity
The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of?
There are two main ways this is handled in the industry:
On-behalf-of: the agent acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent
Fixed credentials: there is a fixed set of credentials that the agent uses no matter who is invoking it (eg a service account)
This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents, Manage connections):
OpenSWE:
When you message it, it acts on behalf of you (eg will open up PRs with your GitHub handle)
When it runs in background (for example, as a code review agent) it acts with its own identity (GitHub app)
GTM Agent:
It has some tools (eg Salesforce access) where it uses a fixed identity, so not everyone has to log in

We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives:
It lives where people already work (for us that's Slack)
It knows who's asking and acts OBO that person for some services and with its own identity for others
It has memory, scoped globally and/or at the user level
Code runs in a sandbox and can make requests to services which require auth

GTM Agent: a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions
OpenSWE: our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs

I'm going to be honest here: I'm writing this because I'm tired of having to explain it, and it seems like there's no single "resource" that properly explains what a harness actually is.
By the end of this article, you should know everything you'd ever need to know about what a harness is and how they work.


Humans use interfaces
Generally speaking, humans don't use computers by writing code. They use an interface of some form, be it a terminal, a website, or an app.
Theoretically speaking, a human could just write unique python or js code for every task they want to complete. Instead of making them do that, we give them access to that code via buttons, hotkeys, commands, etc.
Examples of interfaces: Chrome, Claude Code, ChatGPT App (prev. Codex)
It is also worth noting that humans don't see the code underneath...usually. The human only sees the interface.
LLMs use harnesses
By default, all an LLM can do is generate text. In order for a language model to do anything more, it needs tools. Most llms are now trained to work with tools like "read_file" (for accessing files on your computer), "edit_file" (for changing those files), "bash" (for running commands), and "search" (for finding data online).
The LLM still just sends text though! It can't click a button like a human. As such, we need a custom text format for the LLM to use that indicates "you should run some code". Let's say we give the LLM a format for calling tools, such as:
<read_file name="README.md">
Now the LLM knows it can respond in this format. But it's still just text, it doesn't do anything! Would be like typing on a keyboard or moving a mouse while the computer is off.
Something has to interpret these responses, and then run the right code based on what the LLM responded with.
In order for an LLM to actually do stuff, it needs:
Tools that can do things (read_file, edit_file, bash, search etc)
A special syntax for calling those tools via text
A system that parses the message to identify that syntax and run the code
A method to give the response from the tool back to the LLM
A list of tools available w/ descriptions of how to use them
That is the harness.
"Isn't Claude Code a harness?"
Kind of.
Claude Code has 2 parts: the interface and the harness
When you run "claude" in your terminal, the Claude TUI opens. When you go to the "code" tab in the Claude desktop app, the Claude Code GUI opens. Neither of these are harnesses.
Under the hood, Claude Code uses the Anthropic Agent SDK to interface with the agent. ChatGPT does the same, with the ChatGPT/Codex app interfacing with the Codex App Server (built into the CLI).
I understand why people are confused: Claude Code and Codex both bake the harness into their apps.
You can bake the same harness into other apps though! Some examples of this:
The Cursor harness is used by Grok Bot
The Anthropic Agents SDK and Codex App Server are used by T3 Code
Pi is used by OpenClaw
The harness is a separate piece, rarely if ever exposed to the humans using the apps.
Who owns the tools?
Let's imagine a harness as a kitchen.
Kitchens have lots of different tools. Pots, pans, knives, spatulas, blenders and more.
No kitchen has everything that every chef needs.
Good harnesses are built with this assumption, allowing users to bring their own tools.
To be clear: most of the important tools are provided directly by a harness. Codex and Claude Code both include a lot of tools, while other harnesses like Pi are much more minimal.

The orange box is meant to be "things included by Claude Code" (agents sdk to be clear).
There are lots of custom tools you can add, such as the TypeScript plugin to give your LLM some tools to check your code, or the CUA plugin to allow agents to control your computer.

## What changed
- Harness definition: [L098] Theo's article says a harness is the tools, the call syntax, the parser that runs them, the loop that returns results to the model, and the tool list. It also says Claude Code and Codex bake a harness into their apps. Good harnesses let you bring your own tools.
- Company harness recipe: [L105] LangChain's five components for internal agents:
  - They live in Slack.
  - They have an identity model, either on-behalf-of or fixed credentials, set per tool.
  - They keep memory scoped globally or per user.
  - Code runs in a sandbox that can make authenticated requests.
  - Many runs are scheduled instead of invoked by a person.
- Harness self-improvement: [L089] Google Research's harness² hill-climbs the harness while the model stays fixed.
- Deterministic recipes: [L095] A team open-sourcing its harness turns agentic loops into deterministic workflow-DSL recipes inside a self-improving loop.
- Agent architecture: [L106] Anthropic's "When to fold subagents into your main agent loop" says a single agent with skills often beats a multi-agent setup. I saw this only through a hype repost. Read the original article, not the post.
- Evals:
  - [L090] Hamel Husain's guide to using decision models as LLM judges. It covers choosing the model, tuning the threshold instead of assuming 0.5, and reading the scores.
  - [L094] Cameron Wolfe's roadmap for evals on subjective tasks, with ways to reduce noise.
  - [L091] Letta's FrontierMemory scores agent memory on downstream task performance. Recall benchmarks are saturated.
- Hill-climbing tooling: [L092] Browser Use's open-source rl-env-use builds a verified environment from a one-line skill description.

## Who disagrees
- Subagents: [L106] says to fold them into one agent with skills. [L105] runs several specialised agents, and [L095] adds structure through routing and recipes.
- Who writes the harness: [L089] automates tuning it with a loop. [L105] and [L098] treat it as something you design by hand.
- Where the gain comes from: [L100] says minimizing human attention, with overnight loops, is the main unlock. [L105] puts the work into identity, permissions and UX around the agents.

## What to do
- Read the Anthropic subagent article behind [L106] and test one multi-agent setup of yours against a single agent with skills.
- Use [L098] as the shared definition when you teach harnesses.
- Map your own harness against the five components in [L105]. Identity and scheduled runs are the ones people most often miss.
- Try the hill-climbing loop in [L089] on one harness, with rl-env-use [L092] as the environment source.
- Apply [L090] and [L094] to your judge setup: tune the threshold, and add noise controls for subjective checks.
- Use [L091] if you evaluate agent memory.
